q: A parent partitioned table has no rows of its own. Where do they live, and who routes them?
options: In the partitions, and the database routes inserts and queries, so clients don't change
In the parent's own file, and an index points at each range
In the partitions, and the client has to name the right one
In a shared heap, and a trigger copies rows into each partition
why: That's what separates partitioning from sharding, where the client has to know.

q: A partition is declared FROM (0) TO (35). What's the highest value it holds?
options: 34: the upper bound is exclusive
35: both bounds are inclusive
36: the bound is rounded up
It depends on the column's type
why: The real max(g) was 34. Adjacent partitions can share a bound for that reason.

q: A query with a good index read 46 pages on a plain table, and 46 on the partitioned one. What does that show?
options: The index already narrowed the search, so partitioning added nothing for this query
Pruning was turned off by default
Partitioned tables can't use indexes
The planner ignored the partition's smaller index
why: The course saw the same thing. Its explanation is that the benefit appears when a big index no longer fits in memory.

q: With no index, a range query read 22,124 pages on the plain table and 4,420 on the partitioned one. Why?
options: Pruning left one small partition, so the sequential scan simply read less
Partitions are compressed, so each page holds more rows
Partitioned tables build a hidden index at insert time
The second query reused the first query's cached pages
why: 180 ms against 56 ms. Partitioning shines when a scan can be limited to fewer pages.

q: What does SELECT * FROM grades_parts WHERE id = 7 do on a table partitioned by g?
options: Searches every partition, because the filter isn't on the partition key
Goes straight to the first partition, because ids start there
Fails, because id isn't part of the partition key
Uses the parent's global index on id
why: Pruning needs the key. Partition by what your queries filter on.

q: Why did dropping a year of data take 46 ms where DELETE took 407 ms?
options: Dropping a partition removes a file, and DELETE marks rows dead one at a time
DELETE has to rebuild the partition's index first
Dropping a partition skips the WAL and fsync entirely
DELETE takes a table lock, and DROP doesn't take any lock
why: DELETE also left half a million dead rows for vacuum to clean up.

q: What happens when an UPDATE changes a row's partition key?
options: The row moves to the right partition, as a delete and an insert
The update fails with a constraint error
The row stays put, and a query can't find it again
The partition bounds stretch to fit the new value
why: The real run showed tableoid change from g_low to g_high. Pick a key that rarely changes.

q: Inserting NULL into a range-partitioned table failed. What let it succeed?
options: A DEFAULT partition, which catches rows that fit no range
Casting the NULL to zero in the insert
Declaring the partition key NOT NULL
Setting enable_partition_pruning to off
why: My notes said the column must be NOT NULL. That was the demo, not a rule.

q: What's the largest value of a Postgres int?
options: About 2.1 billion, because it's signed
About 4.3 billion, because it's 32 bits
About 9 quintillion
About 65,000
why: 2,147,483,647. My notes said 4 billion, which would be unsigned.

q: Where should you create an index on a partitioned table since Postgres 11?
options: Once on the parent, and it appears on every partition
On each partition, by hand, in the same transaction
Only on the partition that's queried most
Indexes can't be used on partitioned tables
why: The parent has no real index data of its own. Each partition gets a smaller index.

q: What does vertical partitioning do?
options: Moves a big, rarely read column away, so hot columns pack more rows per page
Splits rows by a date range
Spreads rows over several servers
Stores each row twice, for faster reads
why: Horizontal splits by rows. Postgres does a version of vertical partitioning automatically with TOAST.

q: Why can't a unique constraint on a non-key column be enforced across a partitioned table?
options: Each partition enforces its own, so the constraint must include the partition key
Unique constraints aren't allowed on partitioned tables at all
It would need a table lock on the parent for every insert
Partitions don't support B-tree indexes
why: One partition can't see another's rows, so only keys that include the partition column are checkable.

q: What's the new question that sharding creates and partitioning doesn't?
options: Given a key, which server has it?
Which index should this query use?
How large should a page be?
Which isolation level should each row have?
why: Partitions live in one database that routes for you. Shards are separate servers, so something else has to route.

q: You have 16 servers using hash % N and add one. What share of keys moved in the measurement?
options: About 94%
About 6%
About 50%
None: only new keys go to the new server
why: A key stays only if both remainders match. With a ring it was about 6%.

q: On a hash ring, which server owns a key?
options: The next server clockwise from the key's position
The server closest in network distance
The server with the least data at the time
The server whose hash equals the key's hash
why: So a new server only takes keys from the arc just before it.

q: Why does a real ring give each server many points?
options: With one point the busiest of five servers held 263% over its fair share
It lets a server store each key several times
Clients can then read from any point in parallel
A ring needs at least 64 points to work at all
why: Many points average out the arcs, and spread a departing server's keys over many others.

q: My notes described consistent hashing as hash modulo N. What's wrong with that?
options: Modulo is what consistent hashing replaces, because changing N remaps most keys
Modulo can't be computed on strings
Consistent hashing doesn't use a hash function
Nothing: the two are the same thing
why: The course's later talk on the topic gets this right.

q: A transfer updates two shards, and the second dies between commits. What did the real run end with?
options: 500 in total instead of 600: one side committed and the other didn't
600: the first shard rolled back automatically
600: the second shard replayed the change on restart
An error on both, with nothing changed
why: Each shard commits alone. Nothing ties them together without a protocol such as two-phase commit.

q: A URL shortener is sharded by short code. What does a search by long URL have to do?
options: Ask every server and combine the results
Ask whichever server is least busy
Hash the long URL and ask one server
Use the shard map to find the right index
why: A query that doesn't use the shard key has no way to pick a server.

q: What should you try before sharding?
options: Partitioning, caching and replication, after finding the real bottleneck
Nothing: shard as soon as a table passes a million rows
Moving from B-trees to hash indexes
Raising max_connections until it stops helping
why: Reads scale easily with copies. Writes are the usual reason to shard at all.

q: What's the problem with a serial id on each shard?
options: Each server counts separately, so ids aren't unique across shards
serial is unavailable once a table is sharded
The ring can't hash integers
Serial ids always land on the same shard
why: Use UUIDs, or a key that includes the shard.

q: A hash spreads keys evenly. Why can a shard still get overloaded?
options: One very popular key still lands on a single server
Hash functions favour low-numbered servers
Rings drift out of balance over time
Replicas send their reads to the first shard
why: A hash balances keys, not traffic.

q: What does Vitess do?
options: Sits in front of MySQL, parses SQL, and routes it to the right shard
Replaces MySQL's storage engine with a sharded one
Copies all shards into one server for reporting
Adds cross-shard foreign keys to MySQL
why: It hides sharding from clients, at the cost of one more system to run.

q: The course's first consistent-hashing library failed. How?
options: The same key gave different servers, which broke reads
It was too slow to use on every request
It only worked with numeric keys
It sent every key to the first server
why: The lesson is to verify that a mapping is stable before trusting it with data.

q: A server is removed from a ring after a crash, with no warning. What's the catch?
options: Its keys now map to a neighbour that doesn't have the data, so shards also need replicas
The whole ring has to be rebuilt from scratch
All the keys are remapped, as with modulo
Nothing: the ring copies each key to its neighbour
why: A ring limits what moves, but a crash gives no time to copy anything.

q: What does a Postgres standby actually receive and replay?
options: The primary's write-ahead log
Copies of each SQL statement
A nightly dump of the tables
Row changes decoded into JSON
why: The same log that protects the primary builds the copy, which is why schema changes replicate too.

q: You run CREATE TABLE on a standby. What happens?
options: It fails: cannot execute CREATE TABLE in a read-only transaction
It works, and the table is copied back to the primary
It works on the standby only, until the next restart
It's forwarded to the primary automatically
why: Standbys only replay. That's why replicas scale reads and not writes.

q: Which synchronous_commit setting waits until a read on the standby would see the change?
options: remote_apply
remote_write
local
on
why: It was the slowest in the test, and it gives read-your-writes on the standby.

q: A user saves their profile, and the reload shows the old value. Why?
options: The read went to a replica that hadn't applied the change yet
The commit silently rolled back
The browser cached the page
The write went to the wrong shard
why: With a 2-second delay, the real run showed the primary and standby disagreeing for 2 seconds.

q: With synchronous replication on, the standby's network is cut. What did a client's INSERT do?
options: It waited, with the server showing wait_event=SyncRep
It failed at once with a connection error
It succeeded straight away, and replication caught up later
It was redirected to a different standby
why: That's consistency over availability: no client hears 'saved' for what the standby lacks.

q: You cancel a commit stuck waiting for a synchronous standby. Is the row in the table?
options: Yes: it had already committed locally, and only the acknowledgement was being held
No: cancelling rolls the transaction back
Only after the standby returns
Only on the standby
why: The warning says so. An application treating this as a rollback would be wrong.

q: Under asynchronous replication with the network cut, what do the two servers do?
options: The primary accepts every write, and the standby keeps answering with stale data
Both refuse all requests until the network returns
The primary stops, and the standby takes over
The standby starts accepting writes as well
why: That's availability over consistency. The standby caught up by itself when the network came back.

q: In the failover test, the primary acknowledged 200 orders the standby never got. How many were on the new primary?
options: None
All 200, replayed after promotion
About half, depending on timing
All 200, but marked as unconfirmed
why: All 200 were gone. That's the true price of asynchronous replication.

q: In CAP, what does C mean?
options: A read sees the latest write
The data obeys the rules you declared
Transactions commit in order
All columns have a consistent type
why: The second option is ACID's C. They're different ideas that share a word.

q: In CAP, what does P mean?
options: Tolerating a network failure between nodes
Splitting a table into partitions
The primary being available
Persisting data to disk
why: With more than one node, networks do fail, so the real choice is C or A during a split.

q: Why is a single big server 'CA' in the course's terms?
options: It has no network between copies to fail, so the question doesn't arise until it fails
It keeps two copies of everything in memory
It uses synchronous replication to itself
It's fast enough to hide any inconsistency
why: Where CAP applies depends on where you draw the line around the system.

q: Why does adding replicas not help a write-heavy system?
options: Every standby replays every write, so writes aren't spread out
Replicas slow writes down by locking the primary
Replicas can only be added while writes are paused
Writes are sent to all replicas at random
why: Replication scales reads. Spreading writes takes sharding.

q: Why is one synchronous standby risky?
options: If it dies, all writes stop, so it's a single point of failure
It doubles the chance of data corruption
It can't be used for reads at the same time
It stops the primary from taking backups
why: Use ANY 1 over several standbys, so that one failure doesn't stop writes.

q: What's the course's rule for adding a component to a design?
options: Add it only to fix a failure you can name
Add everything a large company uses, then remove what's idle
Start with a queue, a cache and a load balancer, as a baseline
Add components until each one is under 50% load
why: Start simple and ask what fails. Each box brings failure modes of its own.

q: A queue goes between your servers and the database. What does a client's success now mean?
options: The write was accepted, and it may appear a little later, or fail later
The write is durable on disk
The write has reached every replica
Nothing changes: the client still waits for the database
why: A queue protects the database from spikes, and changes what 'done' means.

q: Why can't a layer 4 balancer route /api and /static to different servers?
options: It only sees TCP packets, and doesn't read the HTTP request
It can only route to one server at a time
URLs are encrypted by the client's operating system
It has no way of connecting to more than one backend
why: A layer 7 balancer can, because it terminates the connection, which means it holds your TLS keys.

q: Why does the follows table have two indexes?
options: One answers 'who do I follow?' and the other 'who follows me?'
Two indexes are needed for a composite primary key
The second is a backup in case the first is corrupted
Postgres needs one index per column in a join
why: Reads far outnumber follows, so the extra write cost is worth it.

q: Counting a celebrity's million followers took 47 ms, as a parallel table scan. What's the design answer?
options: Keep a stored counter, and accept that it can lag a little
Run the count on every view, on a bigger server
Shard the follows table by followee
Show no count for accounts with many followers
why: Nobody can tell 3.2 million from 3.1 million, so a slightly stale counter is fine.

q: Why is the 'am I following?' check cheap enough to run on every profile view?
options: It's one primary key lookup: 4 pages, about 0.2 ms
It's cached by Postgres for the session
It reads a counter stored on the profile
It only runs on the first view of a profile
why: The plan was an index-only scan on (follower, followee).

q: Why does fan-out on write struggle with a celebrity?
options: One tweet means a write per follower: over a second at a million
Celebrities' tweets are too large for the timeline table
Followers read too often for the table to keep up
The tweet table's index can't take that many reads
why: It's cheap for most accounts. That's why real systems pull for the few largest.

q: What does pulling a timeline at read time cost?
options: A lookup per followed account on every read: 53 ms at 5,000 accounts
A write per follower on every tweet
Nothing, once the tweets table has an index
A full scan of the tweets table on every read
why: Cheap to tweet, costly to read. Push is the reverse.

q: What's the drawback of using a serial id as the short URL?
options: Short URLs are guessable, so anyone can walk through them
Inserts are slow because the ids are ordered
Ids can't be used as a primary key
It needs a second index for lookups
why: It's otherwise the simplest and fastest design.

q: Why did 5-character codes clash 436 times in a million URLs, out of about a billion possible codes?
options: The birthday problem: clashes grow with the square of the count
SHA-256 favours some prefixes over others
base64 repeats every 4 characters
Similar URLs produce similar hashes
why: Each new code can clash with every earlier one. 8 characters gave none.

q: A short link is created once and read many times. What's the design consequence?
options: Split the paths: writes go to the primary, reads to replicas near users
Use synchronous replication for every read
Cache writes in the client before sending them
Move the data to a column store
why: A little replication lag on a new link harms nobody.

q: Which part of the Twitter design did the course's sessions never reach?
options: The home timeline
Posting a tweet
Following a user
The load balancer
why: Three features were planned and two were covered, so the timeline section in the post is my addition.
